name: A weapon that changes with the passenger
summary: A vehicle whose weapon, or whole job, comes from whoever is inside. Empty, it has a modest default weapon. When someone boards, either the vehicle swaps its weapon for a vehicle-sized version of the passenger's specialty (a gun, a launcher or a tool such as a repair beam), or the passengers fight out of firing ports with their own weapons. One chassis becomes anti-air, anti-armour, anti-infantry or support depending on who rides it, so the composition choice moves from the factory to the battlefield. The design levers: how many seats count, whether the passenger weapon replaces or adds to the default, who aims it, whose upgrades apply, whether the vehicle must deploy first, how long a swap takes, and what happens to passengers when the vehicle dies.
counterplay: Read the loadout from the roof weapon, then fight it with what that loadout lacks; a passenger without anti-air removes the vehicle's anti-air.
Burst the light chassis: one kill can take out two players.
Out-range firing-port vehicles, whose reach is capped by the infantry inside.
Target the crew rather than the hull: crew-killing shots force passengers out or leave the vehicle open to capture.
Punish the swap: hit infantry while they board or leave, and the vehicle during the swap delay.
Catch deploy-to-fire carriers while they move, and attack fixed firing ports from their blind side.

other_examples.game: extra:Command & Conquer: Red Alert 2 / Yuri's Revenge
other_examples.note: The original: one infantry passenger picks the weapon pod (machine gun, repair crane, sniper rifle, tesla, psychic blast, suicide bomb and more). Only the vehicle's own rank counts, and an elite IFV is very strong.

sources.title: Infantry Fighting Vehicle, Command & Conquer Wiki

other_examples.game: extra:Command & Conquer: Red Alert 2 - Yuri's Revenge
other_examples.note: A heavy carrier whose five passengers fire their own weapons out of gun ports with a range and damage bonus, so the loadout defines the vehicle. The Tank Bunker inverts it: a vehicle parks inside a bunker and fights with its own weapon, boosted.

other_examples.unit: Battle Bus (GLA), Humvee and Combat Chinook (USA)
other_examples.note: The bus has no weapon of its own: its damage and range are whatever the passengers bring. When first destroyed it becomes an immobile bunker whose wounded passengers keep fighting.

sources.title: Battle bus (Zero Hour), Command & Conquer Wiki

other_examples.unit: Overlord battle bunker and Helix bunker (China)
other_examples.note: A one-time add-on choice: a bunker that lets five infantry fire from the tank or helicopter, instead of a gatling cannon or a propaganda tower.
An unarmed carrier whose squads can't fire while it moves; it deploys into a static bunker (or does so automatically when about to die) and then they can.

other_examples.unit: M5 half-track and similar open-topped carriers
other_examples.note: Squads fire out of open-topped half-tracks while protected; the British Kangaroo carries fifteen but only six can fire, so firepower is capped by ports, not capacity.

sources.title: M5 Half-Track Transport, Company of Heroes Wiki
Kangaroo Carrier, Company of Heroes Wiki

other_examples.note: The passengers are the ammunition: its only exit is a man-cannon that fires them over obstacles, and they parachute down, exposed to anti-air.

shooter_analogues.note: Passengers on the benches keep their own kit, so the helicopter's extra firepower depends on who sits there: rockets, repair tools, mines.
A three-seat buggy whose rear rider fights with their own loadout, so the third gun depends on who climbs on; the seat is exposed.
Driver, mounted gunner and a passenger who fires their own carried weapon; a rocket-carrying passenger turns it into an anti-vehicle car.

sources.title: M12 Force Application Vehicle, Halo Wiki

shooter_analogues.note: Each seat owns a weapon or job (driver, gunners, commander), so firepower depends on how many seats are filled and by whom.

player_translation.summary: A cheap, fast two-seat car. Alone, the driver has a modest default weapon. When a teammate climbs in, the roof weapon becomes a vehicle-sized version of their class weapon or tool, and they aim it.
as_user: As the driver you buy a cheap, fast chassis with a narrow but useful default weapon, so you aren't useless alone.

Your power spikes when a teammate climbs into the specialist seat: their class decides whether you become anti-armour, anti-infantry, anti-air or a repair platform. You pick up whoever answers the threat in front of you.
The driver's skill is positioning: kiting, flanking, and keeping the gunner's arc on target.
As the passenger you trade your fragile body for speed, armour and an amplified version of your class weapon, which you aim yourself; the risk is sharing the vehicle's fate.
as_target: Check the roof weapon, the colour of its shots and the loadout icon before committing, then fight it with what it lacks.
It is a high-value, fragile target: burst damage on the light hull can take out two players, and a repair-loaded one keeps their tanks alive.
Watch for swaps: boarding, leaving and the swap delay are when it is weakest and when its threat is about to change.
If it shows a loadout without anti-air, your aircraft can engage it freely.
teammates: A built-in two-player combo: 'need a ride' and 'need anti-tank' calls, and in-field counter-picking without re-buying.
An engineer passenger makes it a mobile repair station that also strips parasites off vehicles, a natural answer to infesters.
Squads rotate specialists through one car as the enemy changes: anti-air when aircraft appear, anti-tank when armour pushes.
Kill credit and score go to both driver and passenger.
controls: Interact enters the nearest free seat; number keys switch seats; the passenger can always leave at once.
Driver: WASD to move; left mouse fires the default weapon only while the specialist seat is empty; a key evacuates the passenger on a cooldown; a toggle locks the seat.
Passenger: mouse aims the roof weapon, left mouse fires, right mouse or Q uses the vehicle-sized class ability (for example a repair beam or a stun).
A ping wheel with 'request ride' and 'request specialist'.
feedback: A distinct roof weapon model for each weapon family, readable from above, plus colour-coded shots and a family icon on the nameplate.
A short, visible and audible swap animation, so enemies see the loadout change.
An empty-seat marker for allies, and the passenger's class icon for everyone.
The driver's HUD shows the passenger's class and health; the passenger's HUD shows the hull's health, the weapon's ammo or heat, its firing arc and the shared-fate rule.
Kill feed lists both driver and passenger with the loadout icon.
changes_from_rts: Passengers are people, not switches: they must aim the weapon or use the tool themselves, or nobody will ride.
Collapse RA3's twenty-odd per-soldier results into a handful of weapon families that enemies can learn from above.
Swaps need a time cost (boarding delay, re-entry cooldown), or the vehicle always has the perfect answer.
Revisit the death rule: RA3 kills the passenger with the car, a double penalty on two people. Eject them hurt instead, or keep it and make the fragility very visible.
The empty vehicle must be playable alone, since one player is the whole unit.
Anti-grief rules: passengers can always leave, drivers can lock seats or evict on a cooldown.

team_play.notes: The vehicle's value depends on which teammate boards it, and the passenger gets speed, armour and a bigger weapon in return.

notes: Needs a general multi-seat system (enter, leave, switch seats, several players on one networked vehicle), which the crew models need anyway.
The driver's movement and the passenger's aim from a moving platform must both be predicted and reconciled in the browser.
Content grows with weapon families: each needs a roof model, a swap animation, projectiles and tuning. Mapping classes to families keeps it bounded.
Tools in the seat (repair, stun, parasite removal) need their own targeting and effects.
Edge cases: a passenger leaving mid-shot, the vehicle dying during a swap, kill credit, whose upgrades apply.
Single combinations can dominate: RA3 patches slowed and weakened the tesla and shotgun results and raised the vehicle's price.
A fast, cheap hull carrying a specialist's amplified weapon can out-trade both parts.
Free swapping lets the vehicle always have the right answer; it needs delays and cooldowns.
Too weak alone makes it unbuyable without a partner; too strong alone makes the passenger optional.
Too many results to learn: per-soldier unique weapons across three factions can't be read at a glance.
Roof weapon differences are small on screen, so colour, projectile shape and an icon must carry the information.
The loadout state must always be visible and honest; a Red Alert 2 trick that disguised a loaded IFV as empty had to be patched out.
Whether killing the vehicle also kills the passenger must be clear to everyone.

variants.name: Class swap
variants.summary: One specialist seat: the passenger's class replaces the default weapon with a vehicle-sized version of its own; empty, the default returns.

variants.name: Tool seat
variants.summary: Some passengers give a tool instead of a gun: a repair beam that also strips parasites, a stun horn, a heal aura or a detector.
variants.seen_in: IFV with an engineer, dog or bear

variants.name: Fire ports
variants.summary: Passengers shoot their own weapons out of ports, possibly with a bonus; the vehicle's output is the sum of who is aboard.
variants.seen_in: Battle Fortress, Battle Bus, half-tracks, Warthog

variants.name: Crewed hardpoints
variants.summary: Each seat owns a fixed weapon or job; firepower depends on how many seats are filled and by whom.

variants.name: Shared fate
variants.summary: A choice of what boarding risks: passengers die with the vehicle, are thrown out hurt, or walk out unharmed.
variants.seen_in: RA3 IFV, Battle Bus, Battle Fortress

variants.name: Modular bay
variants.summary: A one-time purchase decides whether a slot is a passenger bunker or a fixed weapon or aura; the options exclude each other.

variants.name: Anchor to fire
variants.summary: Passengers can only shoot once the vehicle deploys into a static bunker, trading mobility for firepower.

variants.name: Wreck bunker
variants.summary: When the vehicle is destroyed it leaves an immobile bunker from which the hurt passengers keep fighting.

variants.name: Human ammunition
variants.summary: The passengers are the payload: the vehicle launches them over obstacles into the fight, briefly exposed in the air.

variants.name: Vehicle as passenger
variants.summary: A bigger host takes a smaller vehicle inside and fires its weapon with a boost while the small one can't move.

variants.name: Cross-faction hybrids
variants.summary: A passenger from another faction produces its own distinct result, so captured or allied troops unlock hybrid weapons.
variants.seen_in: RA3 IFV result tables for all three factions

adds_strengths.why: Changes role mid-match depending on who climbs in.

adds_weaknesses.why: Alone it has only a modest default weapon, and losing the vehicle can hurt two players.

counters.why: Brings whichever amplified class weapon the fight needs to soldiers who can't outrun it.

countered_by.why: Its light hull falls fast to anti-armour, often taking the passenger with it.
Splash and burst damage can take out two players in one vehicle.

open_questions: Can players of different factions be on one team? If so, cross-faction results become a real feature.
Who aims the passenger weapon, the driver or the passenger? (Recommended: the passenger.)
What happens to the passenger when the vehicle dies: killed, thrown out hurt, or unharmed?
Whose upgrades power the weapon: the vehicle's, the passenger's, or both?

shooter_fit.reason: A built-in two-player combo that uses the seat systems team shooters already have (Battlefield, PlanetSide, Halo) and gives cheap infantry a job all game.
